one_liner: Plain-C17 web framework and app server; about 2.1-2.3x Go net/http's plaintext req/s in one independent suite run.
what_it_does: CWIST is a C web framework plus application server that ships its own HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 (lsquic), WebSocket and WebTransport stack, BoringSSL TLS with a one-call hybrid X25519MLKEM768 mode, and an embedded SQLite ORM. You register C callbacks on an Express-style router (cwist_app_get(app, "/user/:id", fn)) and call cwist_app_listen(); the handler fills a cwist_http_response. It is not a drop-in for Go net/http: it is a different language and API, and you build and link it as a static library.
how_it_is_fast: By default it pre-forks one worker process per online core. Each worker is pinned to a CPU and has its own SO_REUSEPORT listen socket, and each worker runs its own reactor. The reactor uses io_uring through raw syscalls (epoll or kqueue as fallback) as a readiness notifier: it arms one-shot IORING_OP_POLL_ADD and runs the handler synchronously on the woken thread, with no completion-queue hand-offs. An optional IORING_OP_RECV path is also available. Responses are serialized straight into a per-connection output buffer and flushed in batches, and request and response share one arena. Request-line and header scans use SSE2/AVX2/NEON byte search.
when_to_use: You want a C (not C++) HTTP server with high plaintext keep-alive throughput per core, and you can pin its workers to dedicated cores.
Many short, CPU-light handlers on Linux, where the io_uring reactor and prefork-per-core model pay off.
Holding very large numbers of mostly idle connections (SSE, WebSocket, long-polling): the README reports 1M loopback connections at about 244 MB peak RSS in reactor mode.
You need HTTP/3, WebTransport or post-quantum hybrid TLS in C without assembling lsquic, BoringSSL and routing yourself.
You need to link existing C/C++ libraries into the request path with no FFI layer.
when_not_to_use: Production services that need API stability or a track record: the repo dates from January 2026, releases v3.1 to v3.7 shipped between August and September 2026, and the README says minor releases may change public APIs until 4.0.
Latency-SLO work at low concurrency: in the same suite run, CWIST's p99 at 64 connections was about 8.6 ms against net/http's 3.1 ms, even though its median was far lower (0.11 ms against 0.72 ms).
Blocking or slow handlers in the default reactor mode: the handler runs on the reactor thread, so a blocking handler stalls every connection on that worker.

HTTPS-heavy or long-idle keep-alive workloads: the README says the async path covers cleartext HTTP/1.x only, HTTPS still uses the thread-pool model for the request phase, and idle keep-alive connections are not yet reaped by a timer.
Windows targets: only Linux, macOS and BSD are documented.

integration.dependencies: Vendored and built in-tree: BoringSSL, lsquic, libttak, SQLite3, cJSON, uriparser, cnats, multipart-parser-c. System libraries: zlib, zstd, brotli (libbrotlienc/libbrotlicommon). Optional: libnghttp2 (HTTP/2) and libcurl (RDBMS auto-mount probing). The link line also needs -lstdc++, and the suite build installs cmake.
integration.min_toolchain: C17 (-std=c17); GCC or Clang, with a separate tcc profile in the Makefile. The suite built it with Debian trixie's default GCC.
integration.platforms: Linux (io_uring with epoll fallback), macOS and FreeBSD (kqueue). SIMD scans have SSE2/AVX2, NEON, RVV, AltiVec and MSA paths with a scalar fallback. The default Makefile passes no -march, so x86-64 builds use the SSE2 path.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented as a contract. By default it forks one worker process per online core, so globals and in-process state are per worker and not shared. Within a worker, the classic mode (CWIST_C1M_MODE=0) runs one thread per connection, so handlers must be reentrant.

gotchas: The docs and code disagree on the worker count. The README's env-var table says CWIST_WORKERS defaults to 1, but app.c defaults to the online core count; set CWIST_WORKERS explicitly.

An on-by-default response cache, Big Dumb Reply, can replay GET responses. It keys on method and path only, and it learns a response once the handler takes more than 10 ms and returns identical bytes twice. Entries live up to 300 s or 100,000 hits. Only responses carrying Vary are skipped, so per-user GET routes that are slow need Vary. The app.h field comment says this cache is 'never replayed by HTTP dispatch', but app.c serves hits from it.

The library build uses -Ofast with LTO; your own code is compiled with whatever flags you choose. Static linking pulls in each vendored component's license: Apache-2.0 for BoringSSL and cnats, BSD-3-Clause for uriparser and libttak.

The issue tracker shows a run of fixed security bugs in 2026: WebSocket RFC 6455 violations and OOM DoS, JWT algorithm confusion, HTTP/2 'Made You Reset', and a non-rotating TLS session-ticket key. Treat the protocol stack as young code.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: In the same 2026-09-24 suite run, CWIST 3.6 led Drogon 1.9 by about 1.15-1.18x and led Agoo-C by about 2x at 64 connections, but only by about 1.01x at 512. Pick it over those two when you want plain C with built-in HTTP/3, WebTransport and PQ TLS. Pick Drogon (C++) or Lwan when maturity and a longer track record matter more than the last 15%.
verified_claims_summary: Setup: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks run of 2026-09-24 (commit f673364), zrk closed-loop keep-alive load against empty or echo hello-world routes. The server was confined to 4 cores of a 16-CPU x86-64 Linux 7.2 host; the CPU model is unknown because the cpu_name field is hardcoded. Result: CWIST 3.6 (GCC -Ofast LTO build on Debian trixie, first-party-maintained entry app) averaged 148.7k/154.7k/151.2k req/s at 64/256/512 connections, against Go net/http (golang:1.27 image, GOAMD64=v3) at 71.5k/67.4k/67.2k req/s, which is 2.08-2.30x. Both servers were CPU-saturated, and neither had errors.
status_note: Very actively developed: roughly weekly minor releases, last commit 2026-09-25, v3.7 is already out while v3.6 was benchmarked. MIT-licensed with 15 stars, and effectively one lead developer (gg582, 327 commits). Usable via make install, Homebrew or pkg-config, but pin an exact tag.
